key_insight: When experiments produce unpaired X and Y across many environments with few repeats each, the environment labels can act as high-dimensional instruments — enabling identification and consistent estimation of sparse causal effects under suitable regularity conditions.
problem_solved: Estimates causal effects under hidden confounding from unpaired observational blocks (we either observe X or Y per environment), in the regime of many environments but few samples per environment, where standard methods fail.
method: Recast unpaired-environment data as an instrumental variables (IV) problem with the environment index as the instrument (possibly high-dimensional).
Exploit sparsity in the causal coefficient vector (few nonzero effects) and use regularized/penalized IV estimation (e.g., Lasso-style selection in IV stages) to recover effects.
Provide identifiability conditions and finite-sample/consistency guarantees that link number of environments, repeat counts, and sparsity level.
impact: Enables causal effect estimation in modern experimental setups with many small experiments or fragmented data (e.g., lab assays, A/B slices, distributed sensors) where X and Y are never jointly measured; offers a practical route to recover sparse causal signals despite hidden confounding.
visual_elements: Schematic DAG: Environment -> X -> Y, with an unobserved confounder between X and Y, and a note that X and Y are observed in disjoint batches.
Block diagram showing unpaired data layout: many environment blocks, some containing only X, others only Y.
Barplot of true vs. recovered sparse coefficients to illustrate sparse-effect recovery.
Performance curve: estimation error vs. number of environments (showing improvement as environments increase) and vs. repeats per environment.
paper_title: Many Experiments, Few Repetitions, Unpaired Data, and Sparse Effects: Is Causal Inference Possible?
paper_authors: Felix Schur, Niklas Pfister, Peng Ding, Sach Mukherjee, Jonas Peters
